title: Tax and elasticity

predict.q: A sugary drink sells at £1.50 a can; 200 thousand cans a week. The government adds a tax of £0.30 a can. In one market demand is **price inelastic** (few substitutes); in the other it is **price elastic** (many substitutes). In which market does the number of cans sold fall more?

options.s: Both fall by the same amount, because the tax is the same
options.fb: The tax is the same, but buyers react differently: with many substitutes they switch away.
With many substitutes buyers switch away: sales fall from 200 to 152 thousand, against 200 to 180 with inelastic demand.
Reversed. With few substitutes, buyers keep buying; sales fall only from 200 to 180.

options.s: Neither: the firms pay the tax, so sales do not change
options.fb: Firms hand over the tax, but the price rises, so buyers do react. Sales fall in both markets.

task: Move the tax slider from 0 to 0.50 and switch between the two demand curves. Watch the price, the quantity and the tax revenue box.

target.do: Set the tax to £0.30 and look at both demand curves, then press Check.

takeaway: Inelastic demand: sales fall a little, the price rises more, and the tax raises more money. Elastic demand: sales fall a lot.
